prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, which brought time and frequency measurement to unprecedented precision

statement.case_for: I ranked B032 first and B042 second in my opening ballot, and having read all eight ballots I now put B042 first. Optical lattice clocks are the one candidate that seven of eight members ranked, and the support comes from members with very different tastes: Kroll and Lindroth place it first, Olsson and Eriksson fourth and fifth, Mehlig seventh. That is breadth worth taking seriously. On the science, Katori's magic-wavelength idea removed the Doppler, recoil and light-shift limits and, with Ye's work, took fractional uncertainty to about 1e-18, orders of magnitude beyond caesium. The performance has been reproduced and compared by independent national laboratories (JILA/NIST, RIKEN and Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB), the redefinition of the second is being prepared, and the clocks already enable relativistic geodesy and sharper tests of fixed constants and dark-matter couplings. As an instrument builder I know that a number like 1e-18 only becomes believable after years of systematics control and cross-checks, and that work has been done. The attribution is also among the cleanest on the list: a two-person prize where every colleague who proposed laureates named the same two people.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is the one Lindroth and Kroll both raise: lattice clocks may be seen as a metrology advance resting on prizes already given for frequency combs (2005) and ion-trap control (2012), rather than as a discovery in nature, and the redefinition of the second is not yet complete. Ye's contribution overlaps with the comb legacy of Hall and Haensch, and others (Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Bloom) were decisive in particular demonstrations. I would also hesitate over awarding Ye twice in a short span if the thorium nuclear clock matures. By my own criteria, B032 remains a more direct case of a new observational window, but it has support from only three members, source identification is still at the 3-4 sigma level and Olsson rates it as early; I do not want to push it past that evidence.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the ATLAS/CMS Higgs discovery first as an overdue closing of the Standard Model, and also ranks IceCube second as a new messenger, while admitting that singling out three people from two huge collaborations is unresolved.
responses.response: I agree with Ulf on IceCube as a genuine new window, and I am not dismissing the Higgs on scientific merit; it is plainly one of the major discoveries of the era. My difficulty is attribution rather than importance. As someone who has worked in large collaborations, I know a spokesperson or proposal leader is not the person who made the discovery analyses, and Olsson makes the same point. A prize for detector leadership and construction is defensible as such, but then the citation has to be written about the detectors, and the accelerator side would still be unrecognised. Ulf, I would like to hear which of the three you think is the weakest name and whether a detector-centred citation would satisfy you. Until that is settled I cannot place B057 ahead of a cleanly attributable prize.

responses.point: Lindroth puts optical lattice clocks first because Katori's magic-wavelength insight made a near-1e-18 regime possible, but asks whether the committee sees this as a discovery of nature or as an instrument and metrology advance, and whether Ye's comb work overlaps with the 2005 prize.
responses.response: I take the discovery-versus-instrument question seriously, since it is my own standard too. My answer is that the magic-wavelength idea is a physical insight about the atomic structure, not only engineering, and that its consequences are physical: gravitational redshift resolved over millimetres, constraints on drifts of constants. On overlap, the 2005 prize rewarded the comb as a ruler and the 2012 prize rewarded control of single ions; neither recognised trapping thousands of neutral atoms in a lattice at a magic wavelength. I would therefore keep the citation tied to the lattice-clock concept and its realisation, and avoid any wording that credits the comb. Eva, you know the atomic theory better than I do. If you think the earliest demonstrations credit someone besides Katori and Ye, I would like to know before we vote.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first as theory anticipating a new state of matter, with experiment reproduced by many groups, while noting the pairing mechanism and the credit for the lead experimental student remain open.
responses.response: This is the candidate I am best placed to learn about from colleagues, since condensed matter is outside my expertise. The prediction-then-discovery pattern is attractive, and five other members rank it, so I keep it as a serious alternative. My reservations are about timing and credit. The origin of the superconductivity and the correlated states is still debated, so the citation would have to be written for the discovery of the phases and not their explanation, and the experimental credit extends beyond the senior author to Cao and others, as you and Olsson both say. I do not think those problems rule it out, but they make me hesitant to rank it first now. If you and Mehlig can say what in the mechanism could change in the next few years, that would help me judge how early it really is.

responses.point: Olsson ranks spherical-aberration correction in electron microscopy first as an invention that opened sub-angstrom imaging, and asks whether the Krivanek STEM line must be recognised and whether instrumentation fits a physics prize.
responses.response: As a detector builder I am sympathetic to enabling instrumentation, and I think the precedent of the 1986 prize for the electron microscope shows physics prizes can honour such inventions. My concern for B028 is the one you identified yourself: the omission of Krivanek and Dellby from a three-person prize on the corrector is a real attribution gap, not a minor one, and it makes the allocation hard to defend. It was also ranked by only two members and Eriksson put it last, so I do not see the breadth of support that the lattice clocks have. If the committee goes the instrument route, I think B042 has the clearer credit chain and the cleaner scientific consequences. I would be willing to consider B028 again if someone can show the TEM and STEM correction lines can be separated fairly.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks KPZ universality first as a simple mechanism with universal exponents, but he is aware that Parisi is excluded, the exact-solution contributors are uncredited, and he ranks optical lattice clocks only seventh.
responses.response: I cannot judge the mathematical-physics credit chain for KPZ, and I accept your own caution on it. Because you list the omission of the exact-solution contributors as a weakness, the support for B037 in this room is a single first place, which I do not think I can build a prize on. On the clocks, I note you rank them seventh with a worry about discovery versus engineering refinement. I read the evidence as different: independent comparisons across several continents are exactly the kind of confirmation I ask for, and the attribution is not in doubt. I would like to hear whether your reservation is about timing, about the 2005 and 2012 overlap or about the kind of result, since the answer would change what I can do about it in the citation.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts optical lattice clocks as a physical discovery and not primarily as a metrology advance, given the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Whether anyone beyond Katori and Ye has a priority claim on the earliest lattice-clock demonstrations that I cannot assess from the supplied ballots.
Whether Ye should be rewarded for lattice clocks now, given that the thorium nuclear clock (B017) is not on the shortlist but may make a later case for him.
If IceCube is preferred, whether the early AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND leaders have claims that make a Halzen and Spiering pairing unfair.
For B019, what the unresolved superconducting mechanism means for how soon the prize can be given; I rely on condensed-matter colleagues here.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for any shortlisted candidate. I work in PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur, none of which is on the shortlist. I trained at CERN in particle physics and my field is close to IceCube (B032) and the ATLAS/CMS Higgs discovery (B057), but my profile shows no personal or institutional tie to the credited individuals. I rank B032 high in my opening ballot because of scientific taste and I treat that as a possible bias to be tested by colleagues.
